tools.name: web_search_exa
tools.description:
Search the web for any topic and get clean, ready-to-use content.

      Best for: Finding current information, news, facts, people, companies, or answering questions about any topic.
      Returns: Clean text content from top search results.

      Query tips:
      describe the ideal page, not keywords. "blog post comparing React and Vue performance" not "React vs Vue".
      Use category:people / category:company to search through Linkedin profiles / companies respectively.
      If highlights are insufficient, follow up with web_fetch_exa on the best URLs.

query.description: Natural language search query. Should be a semantically rich description of the ideal page, not just keywords. Optionally include category:<type> (company, people) to focus results — e.g. 'category:people John Doe software engineer'.

numResults.description: Number of search results to return (default: 10).

tools.name: web_fetch_exa
tools.description:
Read a webpage's full content as clean markdown. Use after web_search_exa when highlights are insufficient or to read any URL.

Best for: Extracting full content from known URLs. Batch multiple URLs in one call.
Returns: Clean text content and metadata from the page(s).

urls.description: URLs to read. Batch multiple URLs in one call.

maxCharacters.description: Maximum characters to extract per page (default: 3000)

tools.name: execute_blender_code
tools.description:
Execute Python code in the connected Blender instance.

The code runs in Blender's Python environment with full access to ``bpy``.
To return data, assign a JSON-serialisable dict to a variable named ``result``.
Deferred completion via ``check_is_finished`` is only supported by the
interactive addon server, and is rejected in background mode.

tools.name: execute_blender_code_for_cli
tools.description:
Execute Python code in a background Blender process.

Opens *blend_file* with ``blender --background`` and runs *code*.
Assign a dict to ``result`` to return data.

tools.name: get_python_api_docs
tools.description:
Return the Blender Python API docs for *identifier*, or list
modules matching a trailing-``*`` discovery pattern.

*identifier* should be a fully-qualified Python name (e.g.
``bpy.app`` or ``bpy.types.Scene.frame_current``).
The trailing-``*`` forms are supported as discovery entry-points:

- ``*`` enumerates the top-level modules (``bpy``, ``bmesh``,
  ``mathutils``, ``gpu``, ...).
- ``X.*`` enumerates the direct-child identifiers under the
  *X* namespace (``bpy.*`` -> ``bpy.app``, ``bpy.context``, ...).

Both return a ``namespace`` response even when ``X.rst`` would
otherwise resolve to ``exact``; the ``.*`` form lets an agent
force the child listing.

The response always carries ``kind``, ``found``, and ``identifier``.
The remaining keys depend on ``kind``:

- ``"exact"`` (``found=True``): ``<identifier>.rst`` was read.
  Extra keys: ``content`` (RST text), ``examples``. When the
  file exceeds 32 KB, ``content`` is replaced with a dot-point
  summary of the file's top-level definitions (prefixed by a
  header noting the truncation) and ``examples`` is empty -
  re-query individual members for their rendered blocks.
- ``"namespace"`` (``found=True``):
  no ``<identifier>.rst`` but ``<identifier>.<child>.rst`` siblings exist.
  Extra key: ``submodules`` (list of child identifiers).
- ``"definition"`` (``found=True``):
  *identifier* is defined inside a parent RST
  (e.g. ``bpy.props.IntProperty`` lives in ``bpy.props.rst``).
  Extra keys: ``content`` (rendered block), ``examples``.
- ``"partial"`` (``found=False``):
  the parent RST was located but the trailing component isn't defined in it.
  Extra keys:
  - ``parent`` the identifier whose RST was loaded.
  - ``available`` top-level definitions in that RST.
  - ``submodules`` sibling identifiers ``<parent>.<child>`` with their own RSTs,
    filtered to those whose last component contains every character of the missing tail.

  For a toctree landing page like ``bpy.types`` ``available`` is empty and ``submodules``
  is the near-miss list; for a self-contained module like ``bpy.props`` it's the reverse.
- ``"suggestions"`` (``found=False``):
  no direct match, but *identifier* appears as a component of other files.
  Extra key: ``suggestions`` (list of full identifiers).
- ``"missing"`` (``found=False``): nothing matched.

``examples`` (present on the ``exact`` and ``definition`` kinds)
is a list of ``{path, content}`` entries referenced from this documentation.

tools.name: get_screenshot_of_area_as_image
tools.description:
Take a screenshot of a single Blender area and return it as a PNG image.

*area_ui_type* matches the area's ``ui_type``.

*size_limit_in_bytes* caps the image size in bytes.
Zero (the default) uses the MCP message size limit.

tools.name: get_screenshot_of_window_as_image
tools.description:
Take a screenshot of the entire Blender window and return it as a PNG image.

*size_limit_in_bytes* caps the image size in bytes.
Zero (the default) uses the MCP message size limit.

tools.name: get_screenshot_of_window_as_json
tools.description: Return a JSON description of the Blender window layout, areas, active object, and selection.

collections enabled to make it visible.

tools.name: search_api_docs
tools.description:
Full-text search over the bundled Blender Python API reference.

Returns a ranked list of hits. Each hit has:

- ``path``: file path relative to the bundled docs.
- ``text``: the matching paragraph plus ``context``
  paragraphs on either side.
- ``breadcrumb``: the section path containing the hit
  (``Section > Sub-section > ...``).
- ``index``: the hit's position in the result list.
- ``score``: a relevance score; higher is better.

The query is tokenised on whitespace and matched
case-insensitively. Every token must appear somewhere in
the paragraph body, the file path, or an enclosing section
title - in any order. Common English stop-words (``the``,
``a``, ``how``, ``to``, ...) are dropped, so natural
phrasings like ``"how to bake"`` work as expected. Regular
expressions are not supported.

Use ``context`` to pull more surrounding paragraphs into
each hit (symmetric, default 0). Use ``index`` with the
position of a previous hit (same query) to get that hit
alone with its text widened to its enclosing section.

Read-only; consults bundled RST files only.

blender.instructions:
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

# Object Types & Creation

Object types: Mesh, Curve, Surface, Metaball, Text (Font), Armature, Lattice,
Empty, Camera, Light, Light Probe, Grease Pencil.

Creating objects:
  * Operators for standard primitives - handle defaults and collection linking.
  * Data API for procedural/batch creation - avoids side effects (selection changes, etc.).
  * Always link new objects to a collection.
  * Names auto-append `.001`, `.002` on collision - capture references immediately
    after creation, never look up by assumed name.

Delete with unlinking enabled to cleanly remove from all collections.

Prefer non-destructive workflows: modifiers over direct mesh edits where possible,
keeping changes adjustable. Apply or edit directly only when final or unavoidable.

# Transformations & Coordinate Spaces

Location, rotation, and scale are in local space (parent-relative, or world if unparented).

Rotation mode determines which property to use (Euler, Quaternion, Axis-Angle).
Always check rotation mode first - writing to the wrong property is silently ignored.

Coordinate spaces:
  * **World** - global. Use the world matrix for reliable positions.
  * **Local** - relative to parent. Location/rotation/scale operate here.
  * **Object** - the object's own system. Mesh vertices are in object space;
    multiply by world matrix for world positions.

Strategies:
  * The origin is the reference point for location; vertices are relative to it.
  * Apply transforms (especially scale) before geometry-dependent operations
    (booleans, physics) - non-uniform scale causes unexpected results.
  * Set the parent inverse matrix when parenting to preserve visual position.
  * Use the world matrix for world-space reads, not manual composition of
    location/rotation/scale.
  * The 3D cursor is a persistent world-space reference used by many operations.

tools.name: list_toolsets
tools.description: List all available toolsets with names and descriptions.

tools.name: describe_toolset
tools.description: Get detailed information about a toolset including all tool names, descriptions, and input schemas.

toolset_name.description: Name of the toolset to describe. Use list_toolsets to see available names.

tools.name: call_tool
tools.description: Call a tool by name. Provide toolset_name to call a toolset tool, or omit it to call a top-level MCP tool. Use list_toolsets and describe_toolset to discover available tools and their input schemas.

toolset_name.description: Optional. Name of the toolset containing the tool. Omit to call a top-level MCP tool. Use list_toolsets to discover toolset names.

tool_name.description: Name of the tool to call, without toolset prefix. Use describe_toolset to discover tool names and input schemas.

arguments.description: Arguments to pass to the tool. Must match the tool's input schema. Defaults to an empty object.
